chapters.title: Chapter 1: Cap Table Basics for Founders

lessons.title: What a Cap Table Is and Why Founders Must Own It

children.text: Meera and Rohan incorporate a Pune startup on a Monday. By Friday they have agreed a 60:40 split, and it feels settled forever. It is not. Within two years they will hire, promise options, take an angel cheque and raise a seed round. Each of those events changes who owns what. The founders who stay in control of their company are the ones who can see those changes coming, in numbers, before they sign anything. That starts with one document.

body.text: Your cap table is the single source of truth for who owns your company. If you do not understand it line by line, someone across the negotiating table understands it better than you do.

children.text: What a Cap Table Actually Is

markDefs.definition: Short for capitalisation table: a record of every share and every promise of a future share a company has made, who holds it and what percentage of the company it represents.

children.text: A
cap table

is a list of everyone who owns a piece of your company, or has been promised one. At incorporation it is two lines long. By Series A it can run to fifty rows covering founders, employees, angels, funds and instruments that have not yet turned into shares. Most founders keep it in a spreadsheet. Its size changes over time. Its job never does: to answer the question "who owns what, right now, and who will own what once every promise is kept?"

body.caption: TiffinBox Foods Private Limited: cap table on day one (illustrative)

children.text: That is a complete, correct cap table. TiffinBox is fictional, but this is exactly what thousands of Indian private limited companies look like on the day the Registrar of Companies issues their certificate of incorporation. Two founders, one class of shares, ₹10 face value, ₹1 lakh of paid-up capital. The simplicity does not last.
A Cap Table Is a Story Told in Rows
Every row added to a cap table is a decision someone made. Here is how TiffinBox's table grows in its first 18 months.

events.title: Incorporation
events.description: Meera takes 6,000 shares and Rohan takes 4,000. Total: 10,000 shares. Meera 60%, Rohan 40%.

events.title: ESOP pool created
events.description: To hire a head of operations and two engineers, the board sets aside 1,000 shares for employee stock options. No shares are issued yet, but the pool is a promise, so it goes on the fully diluted cap table.

events.title: Angel round
events.description: Three angels invest ₹50 lakh together at ₹4,000 per share and receive 1,250 new shares. The company now has 12,250 shares on a fully diluted basis.

events.title: Seed round term sheet arrives
events.description: A seed fund offers a term sheet. The first thing its analyst asks for is the cap table. Chapter 3 picks up the story from here.

body.caption: TiffinBox fully diluted cap table after the angel round (illustrative)

children.text: Percentages are rounded to two decimals, so the column adds to 99.99%. The totals row shows 100% by convention.

body.title: TiffinBox fully diluted ownership after the angel round (%)

body.text: Notice what did not happen. Meera never sold a single share. She still holds exactly 6,000. Her ownership fell from 60% to under 49% because the company created new shares and promises for other people. That is dilution, and it happens to every founder who hires with equity or raises outside money.

children.text: This is the trade every founder makes. A smaller slice of a company worth ₹4.9 crore (12,250 shares × ₹4,000) is worth far more on paper than a bigger slice of a company worth ₹1 lakh. Dilution is not bad in itself.
Unplanned
dilution is.

content.latex: \text{Ownership \%} = \frac{\text{Shares held by the holder}}{\text{Total fully diluted shares}} \times 100
content.caption: The one formula behind every percentage in a cap table

children.text: Meera after the angel round: 6,000 ÷ 12,250 × 100 = 48.98%. Angels: 1,250 ÷ 12,250 × 100 = 10.20%. ESOP pool: 1,000 ÷ 12,250 × 100 = 8.16%. The numerator for an existing holder stays fixed. Only the denominator grows, which is why every holder's percentage falls together whenever new shares or options are created.

body.title: Rohan's stake after the angel round
body.prompt: Rohan holds 4,000 shares. After the ESOP pool and the angel round, TiffinBox has 12,250 fully diluted shares. What is Rohan's fully diluted ownership? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 4,000 ÷ 12,250 × 100 = 32.65%. Rohan has lost 7.35 percentage points of ownership without selling anything, entirely because 2,250 new shares and options were added to the denominator.

children.text: Why Founders Must Own the Cap Table

Many first-time founders leave the cap table to their CA, their company secretary or, worse, their lead investor. The CA records what already happened. The investor models what is good for the investor. Only you are responsible for what your ownership looks like three rounds from now. Here is why that matters.
Every negotiation starts from it.
Valuation, round size and ESOP pool size all translate into one number: your percentage after the round. If you cannot calculate it yourself in minutes, you cannot negotiate it.
You bear the dilution.
Investors usually negotiate protections for their stake. Founders mostly do not have them. The person most exposed to dilution should understand it best.
Promises become permanent.
A casual "we'll give you 2%" to an early employee or advisor becomes a claim on your company. If it is not on the cap table, it will surface later, usually during due diligence.
Due diligence tests it.
Investors and acquirers check your cap table against the share allotment filings (Form PAS-3) and annual returns (Form MGT-7) on the MCA portal. A mismatch can delay a round by weeks or kill it.
Control lives in it.

Under the Companies Act, 2013, ordinary resolutions need a simple majority of votes cast, and special resolutions need at least three times as many votes in favour as against, which in practice means 75%. Where you sit relative to 50% and 75% shapes what you can decide alone. Chapter 4 covers why percentages alone do not tell the full control story.

body.title: Two founders, same company, different outcomes

columns.label: Founder who owns the cap table
points: Updates it the same day any share, option or instrument is agreed
Models ownership after the next two rounds before accepting a term sheet
Knows exactly how much ESOP is granted and how much is left
Documents every equity promise in writing
Passes due diligence without a scramble

columns.label: Founder who outsources it
points: Asks the CA for the numbers when an investor requests them
Discovers post-round ownership only after signing
Guesses at pool usage and over-promises options
Has verbal promises nobody remembers the same way
Spends weeks reconciling records while the round stalls

body.text: Small percentages of large companies can still be life-changing. When Walmart acquired a controlling stake in Flipkart in 2018, co-founder Sachin Bansal was widely reported to hold a stake of roughly 5%, which he sold for around US$1 billion. After a decade of fundraising, the founders owned single-digit percentages of the company they started. Dilution is the price of scale. The goal is not to avoid it. The goal is to choose it deliberately.

body.label: The other path: Zerodha
body.context: Nithin and Nikhil Kamath built one of India's largest stockbrokers without outside VC money, so the founding family has kept the large majority of ownership. Fewer rounds means fewer rows and far less dilution.

body.title: What belongs on a cap table?
body.question: Which of these would normally NOT appear on a TiffinBox cap table?
options: The unallocated portion of the ESOP pool
A convertible note that will turn into shares at the next round
A ₹25 lakh working capital loan from a bank, with no conversion rights
Preference shares held by the angel investors
body.explanation: A cap table records ownership and claims to future ownership. A plain bank loan is a liability on the balance sheet, not a claim on shares, so it stays off the cap table. The ESOP pool, convertible notes and preference shares all represent current or future shares, so they belong on it.

body.title: Name the effect
body.textWithBlank: When a company issues new shares to other people, an existing shareholder's percentage ownership falls even though their share count stays the same. This is called ___.
body.explanation: Dilution happens because the denominator, total shares, grows while each existing holder's numerator stays fixed.

body.title: The WhatsApp promise
body.scenario: Eight months in, Rohan messages a senior engineer on WhatsApp: "Join us and you'll get 1.5% of the company, we'll sort the paperwork later." The engineer joins. Meera does not know about the message. Four months later, a seed fund asks for TiffinBox's fully diluted cap table.
body.prompt: What problems has this created, and what should Meera and Rohan do before sharing the cap table?
body.modelAnswer:
Problems:
1. An undocumented equity promise now exists. It is a potential claim on the company that is not on the cap table.
2. "1.5% of the company" is ambiguous. 1.5% of issued shares, of fully diluted shares, today or after the seed round? Each gives a different share count.
3. It is unclear whether this comes out of the existing 1,000-share ESOP pool or on top of it. On today's 12,250 fully diluted shares, 1.5% is about 184 options, roughly 18% of the pool.
4. There is no vesting schedule, so the engineer could argue the full stake is owed immediately.
5. The co-founders are not aligned, which a seed fund will notice.

What to do:
1. Rohan tells Meera immediately and they agree a single position.
2. Convert the promise into a formal option grant under the ESOP plan: a fixed number of options, an exercise price and a standard vesting schedule with a cliff.
3. Get the engineer's written acceptance of the grant letter.
4. Update the cap table to show the grant from the pool before sending it to the fund.
5. Agree a rule going forward: no equity is promised without both founders signing off in writing.

children.text: Build Your Own Cap Table Today

body.title: Your day-one cap table
steps: Pull your certificate of incorporation, memorandum of association and share certificates.
List every shareholder with their share count, class of share, face value and amount paid.
Add every promise that is not yet a share: ESOP pool (granted and unallocated), convertible notes, iSAFEs, warrants and any written or verbal equity commitment.
Calculate each holder's percentage on an issued basis and on a fully diluted basis.
Check that share counts match your latest PAS-3 and MGT-7 filings on the MCA portal.
Save it as a dated version and update it the same day anything changes.

body.label: MCA portal: company master data
body.description: Look up any Indian company's registered details and authorised and paid-up capital, and access its filed documents, including allotment returns and annual returns, for a fee.

cards.definition: A record of every share and every promise of a future share a company has made, who holds it and what percentage of the company it represents.
The fall in an existing shareholder's ownership percentage when the company issues new shares or options to others.
Ownership calculated as if every option, warrant and convertible instrument had already become shares.
Shares set aside for future employee stock option grants. It sits on the fully diluted cap table even before any option is granted.
The return of allotment filed with the Registrar of Companies whenever a company issues new shares.
A shareholder resolution under the Companies Act, 2013 that needs votes in favour of at least three times the votes against, effectively 75%.

points: A cap table records who owns every share in your company and who has been promised future shares.
It starts as two or three lines at incorporation and grows with every hire, ESOP pool, angel cheque and fundraise.
Dilution cuts your percentage without you selling a single share, because the total share count grows while yours stays fixed.
Dilution is the price of growth. A smaller slice of a much more valuable company is usually the better outcome, as long as it is planned.
Founders, not CAs or investors, must own the cap table, because every negotiation, promise, control threshold and due diligence check runs through it.
Document every equity promise, keep a dated version and reconcile it against your MCA filings.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the people described in its example are fictional. References to Flipkart and Zerodha are based on public reporting and may not reflect exact current shareholdings. Consult a qualified company secretary, chartered accountant or lawyer before issuing shares or making equity commitments.
